conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one is here, because the emotional roller-coaster of new motherhood is real and very common.

We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-item questionnaire that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; think of it as a quick temperature check for your emotional well-being. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger—then we’d talk together about extra support.

I’ll ask each question in everyday language; you can answer however feels most natural. When we’re done we’ll add things up and talk about what the score means and any next steps that might help you feel more like yourself. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it been mostly easy, sometimes, not very often, or hardly ever?

I can still laugh, but it’s not as easy or as often as it used to be. Maybe a couple of times when my partner did something silly with the baby, but mostly I feel like I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s definitely “sometimes,” not “mostly easy.” I have to remind myself to let go and enjoy the moment, and even then the giggles fade pretty fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Mostly just “sometimes.” I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk—but it’s not that steady “can’t-wait” feeling I used to have. A lot of days I just hope I’ll enjoy them, rather than actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, that happens. When the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m just not doing something right—like I should know exactly what he needs. It’s not constant, but probably a few times this week I’ve gone down that “what did I do wrong?” rabbit hole even when it’s clearly not my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes—like I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing is okay or if that tiny rash is something awful, even though the pediatrician said he’s perfectly healthy. It doesn’t last long, but it pops up out of nowhere a couple of times a day, and then I have to talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick flutter of “what if?” that passes once I take a breath. Nothing that feels like a full-on scare.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes. There are stretches—usually late afternoon when the baby’s cluster-feeding and the laundry’s staring at me—where I feel like I’m barely treading water. I don’t feel completely swamped most of the day, but yeah, a few times this week I’ve thought, “I can’t keep up with all this.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Not really. I get sad here and there, but it hasn’t messed with my sleep—maybe I take an extra ten minutes to drift off if I’m replaying the day, but once I’m out, I stay out.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’ve felt that way a few times this week. Not all day, but there are moments—like when I’m feeding the baby at 3 a.m. and the house is dark and quiet—where this wave of sadness just hits. It usually passes after a little cry, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

That happened twice this week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch for hours, and once when my partner left for work and the house felt so quiet. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just sudden tears that came, then stopped after I blew my nose and took a breath.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤ 3 mo post-delivery (per history)

Symptoms endorsed:
- Anhedonia / reduced enjoyment (Q1-2)  
- Intermittent low mood, crying spells, situational tearfulness (Q8-9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Unprompted worries about infant health; brief "what-if" surges without frank panic (Q4-5)  
- Episodic feeling of being overwhelmed, especially late afternoon (Q6)  
- Sleep initiation mildly prolonged but not persistently disrupted by mood (Q7)  

Patterns:
- Symptoms fluctuate; worse during quiet/alone times  
- No neuro-vegetative signs (appetite/weight not mentioned)  
- No self-harm ideation, intent, or plan (Q10)

Screening significance:
- Meets partial criteria for mild-moderate depressive symptoms (persistent sadness, anhedonia, guilt, crying)  
- Co-occurring anxious ruminations without impairment in daily functioning  
- No safety red flags (denies self-harm, substance use, psychosis)

Risk factors:
- First-time parenting stress, cluster-feeding periods, limited daytime support  
- Absence of protective factors not assessed (partner/family support, prior MH history)

Overall impression:
Elevated screening scores for mood and anxiety symptoms in postpartum context; recommend formal clinical interview (EPDS/PHQ-9) and consideration for brief psycho-educational or therapeutic intervention; safety plan reviewed—return if worsening mood, hopelessness, or any self-harm thoughts.
